name: Iceberg
lede: Iceberg is a clear light blue that entered the color charts in the 1920s and 1930s; the books have almost nothing to say about it as a color.

sections.title: A chart name
sections.body:
Iceberg appears in the ISCC-NBS dictionary of 1955, block 186, and Maerz and Paul's earlier dictionary, whose notes date the entry to 1921 and put it on plate 36 H 4 [1]. The ISCC-NBS plain-language name for it is light blue, only 0.6 units from the swatch [1].

In the 29 color books we read, icebergs appear five times and always incidentally: in a battle scene, a simile, an explorer's discoveries, melting Arctic ice and one answer to an Old English riddle, never as a color [2]. Who coined the color name is undocumented, and the fashionable names of those decades were often borrowed from a mood or a product [1][2].

The nearest named color is [[cornflower]], 6.8 units away [1]. The same chart block holds names such as Airway (1928), Diana (1924), Bounding Main and Della Robbia Blue, a reminder of how many 1920s names stood for one pale blue [1]. In plain words it is a [[light-blue]], a cooler cousin of [[sky-blue]].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Iceberg is a middling color in paint: 71 of 23,781 paintings in our archive (0.3 per cent), 51 by the stricter within-painting lens, more common than 50 per cent of named colors [3]. Its most common role is a mid-tone, in 33 per cent of those 51 [3].

It peaks in the 1800s, in 26 of 8,345 paintings, 1.3 times the baseline, and it is most over-represented in France, 2.6 times, with 22 of 3,443 paintings [3]. The earliest match is a work of 1450 by Andrea del Castagno, a look-alike hue 480 years before the name's first record in our sources, 1930 [3]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so a color match is a look-alike hue and not a pigment test. [3]
